questions.q: What does encapsulation mean?
options: A class reusing code from a parent class
Bundling data with the methods that use it, and hiding the internal state behind them
Having many methods with the same name
questions.why: Encapsulation keeps fields private and exposes behaviour through methods, so the object controls how its state changes.

questions.q: Which of these is runtime polymorphism?
options: A static method called on the class
Calling an overridden method through a parent-type reference
questions.why: With overriding, the method that runs is chosen at runtime from the actual object type. Overloading is resolved at compile time.

questions.q: In Java, which statement about abstract classes and interfaces is true?
options: A class can extend many abstract classes
An abstract class can hold state (fields) and constructors; a class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class
Abstract classes cannot have any implemented methods
questions.why: Abstract classes can carry state and partial implementation; interfaces define a contract, and a class may implement several of them.

questions.q: A Car has an Engine that is created with the car and destroyed with it. Which relationship is this?
questions.why: Composition is a strong has-a: the part's lifecycle is owned by the whole.

questions.q: A Department has Professors, but a professor can exist without the department. Which relationship is this?
questions.why: Aggregation is a weak has-a: the parts can live independently of the whole.

questions.q: In a UML class diagram, what does a dashed line with a hollow triangle mean?
questions.why: A solid line with a hollow triangle is inheritance; a dashed line with a hollow triangle is realization (implements).

questions.q: The Single Responsibility Principle says a class should…
options: Have only one reason to change
Be used by only one other class
Never have more than one field
questions.why: SRP is about responsibilities: one actor or reason to change per class, not a count of methods.

questions.q: You add UPI payments by writing a new UpiPayment class that implements PaymentMethod, without editing PaymentService. Which principle is this?
questions.why: The code is open for extension (a new class) and closed for modification (PaymentService is untouched).

questions.q: Square extends Rectangle, and setWidth() on a Square also changes its height, breaking code that expects a Rectangle. Which principle is violated?
questions.why: A subtype must be usable wherever its parent is expected without surprising behaviour.

questions.q: A Printer interface has print(), scan() and fax(), so a basic printer must implement fax() with an exception. What fixes this?
options: Split it into smaller interfaces like Printable, Scannable and Faxable
Add a default fax() that does nothing
questions.why: Interface Segregation: clients shouldn't be forced to depend on methods they don't use.

questions.q: Dependency Inversion says…
options: Low-level classes should create high-level classes
High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations
questions.why: OrderService depends on a PaymentGateway interface; the concrete gateway is plugged in from outside.

questions.q: order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity() breaks which guideline?
questions.why: Law of Demeter: talk to your immediate collaborators, not to their internals. Ask the order for what you need instead.

questions.q: What goes wrong with a naive lazy Singleton (if instance == null, create it) in multi-threaded code?
options: Two threads can both see null and create two instances
It can never be garbage collected
questions.why: The null check and the creation are not atomic, so concurrent calls can race.

questions.q: In double-checked locking, why must the instance field be volatile?
options: So other threads never see a partially constructed object
So the class can be subclassed
questions.why: Without volatile, instruction reordering can publish the reference before the constructor finishes.

questions.q: Why is an enum Singleton often recommended in Java?
options: It is thread-safe and protected against reflection and serialization creating new instances
It is lazily loaded on every call
questions.why: The JVM guarantees a single enum instance and handles serialization correctly.

questions.q: What is the key difference between Factory and Abstract Factory?
options: Abstract Factory creates families of related objects that must match
Factory can only create one object ever
questions.why: Abstract Factory guarantees consistency across a family, like a dark theme's button and checkbox.

questions.q: When is Builder the right choice?
options: A class with two required fields
An object with many optional parameters, to avoid telescoping constructors
When you need exactly one instance
questions.why: Builder gives a readable, step-by-step way to construct complex objects and can validate before build().

questions.q: With the Prototype pattern, what does a shallow copy do?
options: Copies the fields, but nested objects are shared between the original and the copy
questions.why: Shallow copies share references; changing a nested object affects both. Deep copies duplicate nested objects.

questions.q: You must use a third-party SDK whose methods don't match your PaymentGateway interface. Which pattern helps?
questions.why: Adapter wraps the SDK and translates calls into the interface your code expects.

questions.q: How does Decorator differ from subclassing?
options: It adds behaviour at runtime by wrapping an object, avoiding a subclass for every combination
It removes methods from a class
It only works with final classes
questions.why: Milk + sugar + extra shot is three stacked wrappers, not seven subclasses.

questions.q: Proxy and Decorator both wrap an object. What sets Proxy apart?
options: Proxy controls access to the object (lazy loading, permissions, caching)
Proxy cannot hold a reference to the real object
questions.why: Proxy is about access to an object; Decorator is about adding behaviour to it.

questions.q: A Folder contains Files and other Folders, and size() works on both. Which pattern is this?
questions.why: Composite lets you treat single objects and groups the same way in a tree.

questions.q: Which pattern gives one simple entry point to a complex set of subsystems, like placeOrder() calling inventory, payment and shipping?
questions.why: A Facade hides multi-step subsystem work behind one call.

questions.q: Notification types (Alert, Promo) and channels (Email, SMS) should vary independently. Which pattern avoids a class for every pair?
questions.why: Bridge splits the abstraction from the implementation so both can grow separately.

questions.q: A game draws a million trees but only a few kinds. Which pattern saves memory?
questions.why: Flyweight shares the heavy intrinsic state (texture, colour) and keeps only position per tree.

questions.q: A parking lot must switch between hourly and flat pricing at runtime. Which pattern fits best?
questions.why: Strategy puts each algorithm behind one interface and swaps it through composition.

questions.q: What is a classic follow-up question on the Observer pattern?
options: How to make the subject a Singleton
How observers unsubscribe, to avoid memory leaks from dangling references
questions.why: Forgetting removal keeps dead observers alive and notified.

questions.q: An expense goes to a manager, then a director, then the CFO depending on the amount. Which pattern models this?
questions.why: Each handler approves or passes the request on. Remember to handle the case where nobody approves.

questions.q: How does State differ from Strategy?
options: In State, the states themselves trigger transitions as the object's situation changes
questions.why: State models a lifecycle (Idle → HasCoin → Sold); Strategy swaps an algorithm chosen from outside.

questions.q: Which pattern fixes an algorithm's steps in a base class and lets subclasses override only some steps?
questions.why: export() always runs fetch → format → save; subclasses only change format().

questions.q: You need undo and redo for editor actions. Which pattern is the usual answer?
questions.why: Each action becomes an object with execute() and undo(), kept in a history stack.

questions.q: Which pattern saves and restores an object's state without exposing its internals?
questions.why: The originator creates snapshots; the caretaker stores them without reading inside.

questions.q: In a chat room, users talk through the room instead of to each other. Which pattern is this?
questions.why: A Mediator centralises communication, turning many-to-many links into one-to-many.

questions.q: What does the Repository pattern give you?
options: A collection-like interface for data access, so services don't know how data is stored
questions.why: UserService calls repo.findById(); whether that's SQL, an API or memory is hidden.

questions.q: What is a practical benefit of a repository interface?
options: You can swap in an in-memory repository for tests
It removes the need for a database
questions.why: Tests run fast and isolated against a fake implementation of the same interface.

questions.q: What is Dependency Injection?
options: A class creating its own dependencies with new
Giving a class its dependencies from outside instead of creating them inside
Injecting code at runtime with reflection only
questions.why: The caller (or a container) passes in the collaborators, usually through the constructor.

questions.q: Why is constructor injection usually preferred?
options: Dependencies are explicit, required and can be final, which makes testing easy
questions.why: An object can't be created half-wired, and tests can pass fakes directly.

questions.q: Dependency Injection is a practical way to apply which SOLID principle?
questions.why: Depending on abstractions that are supplied from outside is Dependency Inversion in practice.

questions.q: Where should business rules like 'a user can't place more than 5 orders a day' live?
options: In the service layer that uses the repository
questions.why: Repositories handle storage; services hold the rules, which keeps them testable.

questions.q: What is a race condition?
options: Two threads running on different CPUs
When the result depends on the timing of threads accessing shared data, with at least one writing
questions.why: Unsynchronised read-modify-write on shared state gives different results depending on interleaving.

questions.q: Why is count++ not thread-safe?
options: It is a read, an add and a write, which other threads can interleave
It throws an exception on overflow
It always runs on the main thread
questions.why: Two threads can read the same value and both write value + 1, losing an update.

questions.q: How does AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() stay correct without a lock?
options: It uses compare-and-swap (CAS) in a retry loop
It uses synchronized internally on every call
It copies the value per thread
questions.why: CAS updates only if the value is still what it read; otherwise it retries.

questions.q: When does a read-write lock help most?
options: When every operation is a write
questions.why: Readers can proceed in parallel; writers get exclusive access.

questions.q: What is the trade-off of fine-grained locking compared with one big lock?
options: More concurrency, but more complexity and a higher risk of deadlocks
It removes the need for locks
questions.why: Locking per item lets more threads work at once, but juggling many locks is harder to get right.

questions.q: Thread A holds lock X and waits for Y; thread B holds Y and waits for X. What is a standard fix?
options: Always acquire locks in the same global order
questions.why: A consistent lock order removes circular wait, one of the conditions a deadlock needs.
